The ocean's tides are the rhythmic rise and fall of sea levels, driven mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon and, to a lesser extent, the Sun. As Earth rotates, bulges of water form on the sides facing and opposite the Moon. Most coastlines experience two high and two low tides each lunar day. Local geography, winds, and currents shape the exact timing and height, producing variations ranging from gentle swings to dramatic tidal bores in narrow estuaries.
